analysis.one_liner: Bans manufacturing, processing, and sale of asbestos and products containing it.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the bill 47-1 in November 2019, but it never reached the House floor and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Asbestos is a known carcinogen that kills tens of thousands of Americans each year, largely through workplace and building exposure decades ago. Although many countries ban it, the US still allows limited manufacture and imports. This bill would ban asbestos and products containing it one year after passage, with narrow national-security exemptions, and require companies to report their asbestos use. The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved it 47-1, but it never got a vote on the House floor and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people — especially construction and industrial workers, veterans, and families in older homes and schools — would be protected from future exposure to a known carcinogen that causes mesothelioma, lung cancer, and other fatal diseases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, families, and schoolchildren exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits manufacturing, processing, and distribution of asbestos and any product containing it, effective one year after enactment.

Requires companies that have made or sold asbestos to report to the EPA which facilities were involved, how much asbestos was handled, how it was disposed of, and how many people were exposed — with the reports made public.
Directs the EPA to study how much asbestos remains in homes, schools, and other buildings, who is exposed, and what programs would better protect people from it.

analysis.who_pays: The small remaining asbestos industry — companies that manufacture or import asbestos-containing products such as brake linings and gaskets — plus transitional costs for any manufacturer that would have to switch to alternatives within a year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies still making and selling asbestos products

drawbacks.text: The President could exempt companies from the ban for up to three years, renewable once, on national-security grounds where no feasible alternative exists — a broad escape valve.

The ban applies to future manufacture, processing, and distribution; asbestos already installed in buildings is left in place, with the bill relying only on a study and recommendations to address that exposure.
The one-year effective date would impose quick transition costs on any manufacturer of an asbestos-containing product that lacked a ready substitute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost falls on the few businesses that still make or use asbestos and would have to convert to alternatives within a year, plus possible national-security exemption complications the President could manage. Against that, asbestos still causes tens of thousands of cancer deaths in the US each year, and the ban also covers imported products — a real, one-time public-health gain. The reporting and legacy-asbestos study provisions add public visibility at modest expense. On balance the benefits clearly outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: A House subcommittee and then the full Energy and Commerce Committee approved it 47-1, but it was never brought to the full House for a vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in March 2019 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor Committees.
A House subcommittee held hearings in May 2019 and approved it to the full committee by voice vote in September 2019.
The full Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a 47-1 vote in November 2019.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a vote on the House floor and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that still profit from manufacturing, importing, or selling asbestos products — including imported brake pads and other consumer goods — kept operating as before, since the US continues to allow some asbestos imports.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Businesses still importing and selling asbestos products

sides.party_line_note: The 47-1 committee vote suggests broad bipartisan support, but the floor never voted, and nearly all 49 cosponsors were Democrats.

industries.note: The bill bans making, processing, or selling asbestos and asbestos-containing products, eliminating the industry's domestic business within a year, with only narrow national-security exemptions available.

industries.industry: Importers of asbestos-containing consumer goods (brake pads, gaskets, building materials)
industries.note: Imports of asbestos-containing products would be barred, forcing a switch to substitutes; consumers would benefit from products without a known carcinogen.

industries.industry: Abatement, environmental testing, and hazardous-waste firms
industries.note: Mandatory reporting, a federal building survey, and eventual removal work would expand demand for asbestos inspection and disposal services.
